Title: BattleInTheSky: A Low‐Cost Gamified Expert System for Explainable Artificial Intelligence Education

ABSTRACT
Expert systems are a core branch of Artificial Intelligence (AI), but they are often taught through abstract theory that hinders
students' understanding and motivation. This study presents BattleInTheSky, a gamified expert system implemented on the
low‐cost Raspberry Pi Pico W microcontroller using MicroPython. Designed as a hands‐on learning tool for Mechatronics
Engineering students, the system uses IF–THEN rules to control hardware components including buttons, an OLED display,
and a buzzer. It stores gameplay statistics locally and optionally uploads data remotely, providing an interactive experience that
connects AI theory to practical applications. The project integrates symbolic AI, embedded programming, gamification, and
principals of ethical design. It was implemented through a constructivist learning sequence in a sixth‐semester Expert System
course, guiding students from basic hardware control to the design of fully functional expert systems. A mixed‐methods
evaluation assessed technical performance and educational impact. Results showed that students improved their understanding
of expert systems by 22.4% (Cohen's d = 1.3) and reported high motivation (mean 4.0/5). Technical evaluation confirmed the
system's reliability, responsiveness, and usability in classroom settings. The project also fostered ethical reflection through rule
transparency and responsible decision‐making logic. BattleInTheSky demonstrates how low‐cost, transparent, and rule‐based
AI systems can promote accessible and engaging AI education. The approach illustrates how transparent, rule‐based systems
can support explainable and accessible engineering and computing courses, particularly in resource‐constrained contexts.

Introduction
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming industries and societies,
yet its integration into higher education remains fraught with
challenges, particularly in engineering disciplines where practical
application is paramount. Traditional AI education often empha-
sizes abstract theoretical concepts, such as complex algorithms
and machine learning models, which can hinder students' ability
to grasp their real‐world implications [1]. Moreover, reliance on
high‐end computational resources and proprietary software cre-
ates barriers for students in under‐resourced institutions, exacer-
bating digital inequities [2]. These challenges are especially
pronounced in Mechatronics Engineering, where students must
bridge AI theory with embedded systems and hardware integra-
tion, requiring accessible, hands‐on learning experiences that
foster both technical proficiency and ethical awareness.
To address these gaps, this study presents BattleInTheSky, an
innovative didactic tool designed to teach expert systems and
embedded programming to Mechatronics Engineering students.
While previous research has explored using microcontrollers for
computational thinking and expert systems projects, according
to the reviewed literature, our study is the first to integrate a
gamified expert system into a single, low‐cost platform using
the Raspberry Pi Pico W. By uniting symbolic AI logic,
embedded programming, and a tangible, gamified interface,

features position BattleInTheSky as a distinct contribution to
explainable AI pedagogy within engineering education.
This study proposes a multidimensional framework for acces-

assessment strategies. It details the design and implementation
of BattleInTheSky in a sixth‐semester Mechatronics course,

Literature Review
In recent years, the integration of AI into educational en-
vironments has attracted increasing academic attention, driven
by the transformative potential of these technologies in shaping
learning processes. As educational institutions explore the
incorporation of AI tools and concepts into curricula, it
becomes essential to examine existing approaches, identify their
limitations, and highlight emerging strategies that promote
more inclusive and responsible AI education. This literature
review critically examines the current landscape of AI educa-
tion, with a particular focus on accessibility, ethical considera-
tions, and pedagogical effectiveness.
The rapid proliferation of AI tools in educational contexts un-
derscores the urgent need for accessible, ethically sound, and
pedagogically robust frameworks that democratize AI literacy.
However, traditional AI education often relies on high‐end
computational resources, abstract theoretical content, and dis-
connected learning experiences that can exclude learners from
under‐resourced backgrounds.
2.1
|
Expert Systems in Artificial Intelligence
Expert systems represent a symbolic AI paradigm that leverages
explicit, human‐readable knowledge representations in the
form of rules and facts to emulate expert‐level decision‐making
[3]. Their architecture typically includes a knowledge base, an
inference engine, and a user interface. Logical formalisms such
as propositional and predicate logic underpin the rule structures
within these systems, which use inference mechanisms, for-
ward chaining, and backward chaining, to derive conclusions
from inputs [3]. Expert systems offer transparent, rule‐based
reasoning ideal for education, unlike opaque machine learning
models, though less scalable [4]. Their deterministic nature
aligns well with educational settings, particularly in developing
Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS) that simulate domain‐
specific guidance.
The integration of expert systems into educational settings has
garnered increasing empirical support, particularly in fostering
computational thinking and AI literacy among diverse learners.
Grounded in constructivist principles and supported by embo-
died cognition theory [5], these interventions have demon-
strated
tangible
improvements
in
engagement
and
self‐
regulated learning [6]. Udvaros et al. [7] conducted a quasi‐
experimental study in Greece, where secondary students used
microcontrollers to build expert systems for environmental
monitoring,
reporting
an
18%
increase
in
computational
thinking scores (p < 0.01). Similarly, Mustofa et al. [8] found
that microcontroller‐based expert system projects improved
problem‐solving and engagement in an Earth Science course.
These case studies highlight the capacity of expert systems to
bridge theoretical AI knowledge with practical applications.
Despite these benefits, challenges in implementation persist.
Teachers often require additional training to scaffold open‐
ended activities, and initial costs, though modest, may pose
barriers for under‐resourced institutions [9]. Nevertheless,
strategies such as teacher codesign and scaffolded instructional
modules have been shown to mitigate these limitations and
support sustainable integration.
2.2
|
Embedded Programming and Raspberry
Pi Pico W
Embedded programming offers a tangible entry point into
computing principles, closely aligned with educational frame-
works grounded in constructivism and constructionism. Ac-
cording to Piaget [10], learners construct knowledge through
active engagement with their environment, a view comple-
mented by Vygotsky's [11] sociocultural theory, which empha-
sizes the role of guided learning in social contexts. Building on
these foundations, Papert's [12] constructionism highlights the
importance of creating tangible artifacts, such as programmable
devices, as a means of deepening understanding through
meaningful, hands‐on activity.
The Raspberry Pi Pico W offers an ideal platform for im-
plementing these theories. As a low‐cost, WiFi‐enabled micro-
controller, it enables the design of interactive, real‐world systems
that engage learners in coding, debugging, and iterative design.
Hu [13] provides empirical evidence that microcontroller‐based
learning environments increase student engagement, promote
system‐level thinking, and bridge abstract concepts with concrete
applications. Alam [1] and Gabriel [2] further argue that

affordable edge devices like Pico W are critical in expanding AI
education to marginalized contexts.
The embodied cognition perspective [5] supports these peda-
gogical benefits, suggesting that physical interaction with
learning environments enhances cognitive processing. Em-
bedded systems make algorithmic concepts visible and manip-
ulable, fostering deeper conceptual internalization. Real‐world
deployments, such as sensor‐based expert systems for environ-
mental monitoring, demonstrate how students not only learn
code but also engage with design thinking and system dynam-
ics. Despite these benefits, challenges remain in scaffolding
complex tasks appropriately and ensuring equitable access to
necessary peripherals [9].
Empirical studies provide strong support for the use of Raspberry
Pi Pico in embedded programming education. Davidson et al.
[14] implemented a blended laboratory design for first‐year
university students, where learners engaged with Raspberry Pi
Pico to develop interactive digital circuit projects, including a
traffic light controller system. Analysis of student performance
demonstrated significant improvements in understanding digital
logic concepts, as well as enhanced collaborative problem‐solving
and self‐directed learning. Reflections and feedback from stu-
dents highlighted increased confidence, ownership of learning,
and alignment with constructionist educational principles that
emphasize learning through hands‐on creation and exploration.
Similarly, Doropoulou et al. [15] conducted a longitudinal study
in US community colleges, incorporating Pico W‐based AI kits
into introductory courses. Students engaging in embedded ex-
pert systems projects outperformed peers in control groups
using theoretical content, with a moderate effect size (Cohen's
d = 0.62) in final assessments. Structured peer‐review cycles
further enhanced metacognitive awareness, aligning with the
framework's emphasis on reflective practice and system‐level
thinking. These findings validate the Raspberry Pi Pico W as a
powerful tool for democratizing AI education, particularly in
resource‐constrained settings, and underscore its role in oper-
ationalizing constructivist and constructionist pedagogies.
2.3
|
Gamification in Education
Gamification, the application of game elements in nongame
contexts, has shown significant promise in educational settings
when aligned with sound pedagogical theories [16]. Self‐
Determination Theory (SDT) posits that intrinsic motivation is
cultivated when learners feel competent, autonomous, and
socially connected. Gamified systems that provide meaningful
goals, narrative progression, and learner choice have been
shown to enhance engagement and persistence [17]. Cognitive
Load Theory emphasizes avoiding extraneous cognitive load, as
poorly designed gamification can distract from learning objec-
tives [18]. Effective gamification balances motivational affor-
dances with instructional clarity, using progressive challenge
systems aligned with curricular content [19].
Critical literature warns against superficial gamification, which
may fail to support deeper understanding [20]. However,
empirical
studies
show
that
well‐designed
gamified
AI
activities, such as programming challenges, enhance algorith-
mic thinking [21].
Likewise, Gamarra et al. [19] found that gamified engineering
education
increased
engagement
and
retention,
while
Alsawaier [21] found that rule‐based programming challenges
boosted intrinsic motivation among secondary students. These
findings align with SDT's emphasis on autonomy and compe-
tence, reinforcing the theoretical argument that gamification
fosters sustained engagement.
Similar results have been observed in other hardware‐oriented
educational domains. For example, recent studies in hardware
security education have shown that gamified laboratory ex-
periences promote higher engagement and conceptual retention
among engineering students [22, 23]. These works align with
our approach by demonstrating how interactive, game‐based
environments
can
enhance
technical
learning
outcomes
through experiential and motivational design.
2.4
|
Accessibility of AI Education
Equitable access to AI education is a central concern, as
structural inequities such as limited internet access, under-
funded schools, or lack of teacher expertise often constrain
opportunities for learners in resource‐limited contexts [24].
Open‐source hardware and software help mitigate these barri-
ers by reducing costs and enabling scalable, community‐
supported learning environments [25–27]. The Raspberry Pi
Pico W exemplifies such accessibility: its affordability and ex-
tensive online documentation facilitate deployment in diverse
educational settings. Empirical studies highlight how low‐cost
microcontrollers combined with tailored pedagogy can enhance
computational literacy and problem‐solving even in constrained
environments [2, 13, 28] (Panjwani 2024).
Although accessibility involves more than just affordability, this
study emphasizes the technological dimension, showing how
open‐source, low‐cost platforms can reduce entry barriers for AI
education. Previous work with Pico W‐based kits in under-
served institutions has reported significant gains in AI literacy
and learner confidence [15], reinforcing the potential of such
platforms to democratize AI learning. While issues of cultural
adaptation, diversity, and participatory design remain impor-
tant considerations for future research, the present study fo-
cuses on the contribution of affordability and transparent rule‐
based systems to making AI education more widely attainable.

Methods and Materials
This study employed a design‐based research approach to
develop, implement, and evaluate BattleInTheSky, a gamified
expert system designed to teach symbolic AI and embedded
programming in undergraduate engineering education. The
methodology integrates constructivist and constructionist ped-
agogies with technical prototyping and mixed‐methods eva-
luation, enabling a multidimensional understanding of the
system's educational and technical effectiveness.

3.1

Participants and Context
The intervention was conducted during the spring 2025 term in a
sixth‐semester “Expert Systems” course at a university in Mexico.
Fifteen Mechatronics Engineering students participated, organized
into eight development teams (seven pairs and one solo participant).
3.2
|
Instructional Design
The didactic strategy followed a progressive, hands‐on learning
model grounded in constructivism [10], constructionism [12],
and SDT [16]. Over seven instructional phases, students deve-
loped increasingly complex expert systems using the Raspberry
Pi Pico W and MicroPython, culminating in the implementation
of BattleInTheSky, an interactive game with real‐time rule‐
based logic and local/remote data storage.
3.3
|
Technical Evaluation
To assess system performance, a structured technical evaluation
was conducted across nine fully assembled prototypes. Key
metrics included boot time, input latency, memory usage,
OLED response time, error rate, and WiFi connectivity. Data
were collected using embedded tools (e.g., utime.ticks_diff(),
micropython.mem_info()) and manual observations, following
the best practices for UX evaluation [29].
3.4
|
Educational Evaluation
To evaluate the impact of BattleInTheSky on student learning,
motivation, and perceived usefulness, a mixed‐methods approach
was employed during a 10‐week intervention with 15 students en-
rolled in Mechatronics Engineering. The students, organized into
eight development teams (seven pairs and one solo participant),
designed and implemented gamified expert systems using the
Raspberry Pi Pico W. The solo participant's artifact was evaluated
using the same criteria as team projects to ensure consistency.
Four evaluation instruments were developed based on Albert
and Tullis [29], ensuring alignment with learning objectives and
methodological rigor:
• Pre‐/Posttest (Individual): A 20‐question test (10 multiple‐
choice,
5
short‐answer,
5
problem‐solving)
assessed
knowledge of expert systems, inference engines, and ex-
plainable AI. Items were mapped to Bloom's taxonomy, and
results were treated as interval data for statistical analysis.
• Motivation Survey (Individual): A 15‐item, 5‐point Likert
scale instrument based on SDT measured intrinsic moti-
vation, competence, and autonomy. Questions were bal-
anced to reduce response bias.
• Usefulness Survey (Individual): A 10‐item Likert scale plus
two open‐ended questions.
• Game Artifact Evaluation (Team): Projects were assessed
using a rubric with four dimensions, Rule Logic, Code
Clarity, Functionality, and Design, scored from 1 (poor) to 5
(excellent). Rubrics were pilot‐tested to enhance reliability.
3.5
|
Ethical Considerations
The study adhered to the ethical guidelines for educational AI
research. Student data were anonymized and stored locally on
devices, with optional remote upload based on informed con-
sent. The project emphasized transparency in rule‐based system
design, allowing students to directly observe how decisions
were derived from explicit IF–THEN structures.
4
|
Design of Didactic Experience: BattleInTheSky
The design of the didactic project BattleInTheSky in the “Expert
Systems” course was the result of a teaching–learning strategy
grounded in constructivist principles, meaningful gamification,
and technological accessibility. This strategy, applied with sixth‐
semester students in the Mechatronics Engineering program,
enabled the recovery of programming competencies after sev-
eral semesters without exposure to coding languages. The pro-
gression of activities was intentionally designed, aligning with
the theoretical framework Integrating Expert Systems and Ga-
mification via Raspberry Pi Pico W for Accessible AI Education,
aiming to build tangible, contextualized, and pedagogically
robust learning experiences. This strategy resulted in a 22.4%
learning gain and high motivation scores (mean 4.0/5).
4.1
|
Phase 1: Introduction to Hardware and
Algorithmic Thinking
The initial activity consisted of turning an LED on and off using
the Raspberry Pi Pico W microcontroller. This allowed students
to reengage with basic programming concepts through direct
manipulation of hardware. From a constructivist perspective,
and embodied cognition, this activity laid the foundation for a
progressive understanding of computational logic, activating a
sense of control, curiosity, and personal agency, in line with the
principles of SDT [16].
4.2
|
Phase 2: Introduction to Fact Bases and
Sensing
The second stage introduced data structures (Python dictio-
naries) to simulate a fact base within expert systems. Students
integrated sensors and developed their first IF–THEN rules,
approaching the fundamentals of symbolic knowledge repre-
sentation [3]. This phase marked the transition from abstract
coding to tangible computing, reinforcing the notion of systems
that react to environmental conditions.
4.3
|
Phase 3: Inference Engines and Multiple
Sensors
The third activity introduced chained inference engines, inte-
grating both temperature and light sensors. Students developed
logic that responded to multiple conditions, exercising skills in
logical inference and symbolic reasoning. This stage encouraged
reflection on the scalability and maintainability of expert

Phase 4: First Autonomous Expert System
In this phase, students built an expert system that responded to
environmental conditions using LEDs and, optionally, an OLED
display. This activity strengthened the understanding of the
sense‐decision‐action cycle, while introducing the concept of
explainable interfaces in an accessible manner [31]. The OLED
display was offered as an optional component to ensure equi-
table access to resources, consistent with principles of techno-
logical accessibility [2].
4.5
|
Phases 5: Full Implementation of
BattleInTheSky
The final activity represented the full integration of previous
learning. In BattleInTheSky, students designed a gamified expert
system controlled by IF–THEN rules, with input sensors (buttons),
actuators (OLED, buzzer), local data storage, and remote connec-
tion to an online database. This fulfilled principles of transparency,
traceability, and responsible technological integration [32].
The sixth activity introduced WiFi connectivity and remote
storage, exposing students to foundational concepts in cloud‐
based educational computing and distributed system resilience.
Lastly, the seventh activity focused on a technical and opera-
tional evaluation of the system, assessing metrics such as
latency, robustness, scalability, and code clarity, thereby fos-
tering a culture of continuous improvement and performance‐
based evaluation [15].
Beyond technical and pedagogical aspects, the instructional
strategy incorporated a cross‐cutting reflection on the respon-
sibility involved in designing decision‐making rules. Critical
analysis was encouraged regarding potential failures, biases in
condition programming, and unforeseen consequences. This
ethical dimension drew inspiration from proposals on algo-
rithmic transparency and explainability [31, 33], recognizing
that even simple systems can pose risks if not designed with
clarity and robustness.
The didactic strategy used to implement BattleInTheSky not
only facilitated the progressive development of skills in expert
systems and embedded programming, but also exemplified an
inclusive, critical, and technically sound educational practice.
The underlying theoretical framework provided pedagogical
coherence, while the practical implementation confirmed that
AI learning can be accessible, ethical, and motivating, even in
resource‐constrained environments.

System Description
As part of the BattleInTheSky educational experience, students
designed and implemented a fully functional embedded expert
system that simulates a gamified decision‐making environment.
The resulting console integrates physical inputs and outputs
with rule‐based logic, local data storage, and optional remote
connectivity, enabling a tangible and interactive learning pro-
cess rooted in symbolic AI.
The system is built around the Raspberry Pi Pico W, a low‐cost,
WiFi‐enabled microcontroller programmed in MicroPython. It
features three tactile buttons for directional input and firing, a
128 × 64 SSD1306 OLED display for real‐time visual feedback, and
a passive buzzer for audio cues. Power is supplied by a 3.7 V LiPo
battery, and the components are assembled on a breadboard or
housed in custom casings, depending on team preferences,
allowing flexibility while maintaining a standardized architecture.
The software architecture includes a rule engine that processes IF–
THEN logic, drivers for the OLED display, and optional modules
for WiFi‐based data uploads. Core functionality is managed
through main.py, with supporting scripts such as ssd1306.py and
secrets.py, and performance metrics stored locally in stats.txt. The
system handles network failures gracefully to ensure data per-
sistence and usability in varied connectivity contexts.
Functionally, the console operates as a gamified expert system:
button inputs trigger logic‐based decisions that affect game
state, such as avatar movement, projectile launches, and colli-
sion detection. Feedback is delivered through synchronized
visual and auditory responses. The system supports both local
and remote storage of player data and is designed for modular
expansion, allowing students to iterate on the rule base, inte-
grate additional sensors, and deepen their understanding of
embedded AI systems.
5.1
|
Game Mechanics
BattleInTheSky operates as a gamified expert system where
students interact through three physical buttons mapped to IF–
THEN rules, triggering actions such as avatar movement, pro-
jectile launches, and collision events. This interaction exposes
students to the structure of symbolic AI, including rule‐based
knowledge bases, inference engines, and decision outputs,
through direct, observable system behavior. Events like colli-
sions or scoring are also rule‐driven, reinforcing the logic‐
driven architecture, and encouraging students to debug, extend,
and reflect on their rule designs.
This tangible interaction bridges theory and practice, enabling
students to internalize expert system concepts via a closed‐loop
control model. Rather than learning inference in abstraction,
students experienced symbolic reasoning by iteratively coding,
testing, and observing outcomes in real time. The hands‐on
approach promoted engagement, system‐level thinking, and
metacognitive development, as evidenced by strong artifact
performance and student feedback.

Results
6.1
|
Technical Evaluation
To assess the technical viability and operational performance of
BattleInTheSky, a structured evaluation was carried out across
nine fully assembled systems built by student teams. Each
system adhered to a common architecture based on the Rasp-
berry Pi Pico W and included three tactile push buttons, an
SSD1306 OLED display, a passive buzzer, and a battery‐
powered circuit with a regulated power switch (Figure 1). The
evaluation was conducted during classroom sessions between
March and May 2025.
Each team consisted of two students, who participated in testing
under real‐world classroom conditions, with indoor tempera-
ture averaging 30°C–34°C, due to the regional climate of the
city. WiFi connectivity was consistently available throughout
testing sessions.
Measurements were conducted using embedded tools such as
utime.ticks_diff()
for
latency
analysis,
and
micro-
python.mem_info()
for
memory
profiling.
Manual
tools,
including a stopwatch, were used to measure boot‐up time and
OLED response latency. Runtime metrics and system behaviors
were observed using the Thonny IDE's serial console. Per-
formance metrics were selected based on user experience eva-
luation principles [29], ensuring robust assessment.
Runtime performance metrics were collected across multiple
gameplay sessions per team in order to evaluate system
responsiveness and stability. These metrics encompassed boot‐
up time, memory usage, input latency, OLED refresh behavior,
error rates, WiFi connection success, and battery duration.
Table 1 summarizes the key quantitative results. Overall, sys-
tems exhibited quick startup times (average 2.1 s), low runtime
memory usage (~14 KB used), and responsive input‐action
cycles, with latencies ranging between 12 and 27 ms.
To further illustrate consistency across prototypes, Figure 2
presents a bar graph comparing input latency for the nine tested
systems. The narrow range of latencies observed highlights the
reliable performance of the button‐to‐action interaction cycle
under real‐world classroom conditions.
Additionally, OLED updates were near‐instantaneous with no
reported visual flickering, and error rates remained negligible
across all tests. WiFi connections were consistently established
within 3–5 s, and remote upload success was achieved in 80% of
attempts, with local logs preserving data when necessary. Bat-
tery runtime, while not extensive, was sufficient for casual
classroom use.
These findings collectively demonstrate that BattleInTheSky
achieved
its
intended
goals
of
operational
stability
and
responsive gameplay experience under practical conditions.

Educational Evaluation
6.2.1

Learning Outcomes (Pre‐/Posttest)
All participants demonstrated significant learning gains, with
an average improvement of 22.4% (from 68.0 ± 4.8 to 83.2 ± 4.2;
p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 1.3). Several items within the test ex-
plicitly targeted explainable AI concepts such as rule transpar-
ency
and
ethical
decision‐making,
and
the
observed
improvement in these items reflected students' deeper under-
standing of how AI systems make decisions. The highest gains
were observed in problem‐solving questions (+5.8 points), fol-
lowed by short‐answer (+4.2) and multiple‐choice (+3.1),
indicating strong development of applied skills. The solo par-
ticipant (Team 8) improved from 73 to 87, in line with team
averages.

Game Artifact Evaluation
Team artifacts scored well across all dimensions (out of 5):
• Rule Logic: 4.0 (SD = 0.8).
• Code Clarity: 3.9 (SD = 0.7).
• Functionality: 4.1 (SD = 0.7).
• Design: 3.9 (SD = 0.6).
As shown in Table 3, the highest‐scoring project (Team 8)
received 19/20, while the lowest (Team 6) received 12/20, due to
functionality issues. A moderate positive correlation (r = 0.62,
p = 0.015) was found between team‐averaged posttest scores
and artifact scores, suggesting that individual learning en-
hanced team outcomes. Interestingly, the solo participant, who
also scored among the highest in the posttest, achieved the top
score in the artifact evaluation, suggesting that smaller teams
may promote greater accountability and deeper engagement.
This observation aligns with the principles of SDT. A lone
learner might experience an elevated sense of autonomy and
competence, as they are solely responsible for all design and
implementation decisions. This finding, while based on a small
sample, provides a valuable direction for future research on the
role of team size and student dynamics in project‐based learn-
ing. Educators could explore tailored instructional strategies
that balance collaborative and individual work to maximize
learning outcomes.
As summarized in Table 4, students demonstrated substantial
learning gains, with posttest scores improving by over 15 points
on average compared to pretest results. Motivation and per-
ceived usefulness also remained consistently high (above 4.0 on
a 5‐point scale), and the mean artifact score reflected solid
performance across teams. These combined results reinforce the
gamified expert system's effectiveness in fostering knowledge
acquisition and positive learning experiences.

used microcontrollers for educational purposes, our project
introduces a novel approach by embedding symbolic AI
decision‐making within a self‐contained, gamified console. This
unique blend of ule‐transparency, tangible interaction, and
ethical reflection distinguishes our work and provides a deeper,
multisensory learning experience. Students exhibited significant
learning gains in expert system concepts (22.4% improvement,
d = 1.3), alongside high levels of intrinsic motivation (M = 4.07)
and perceived usefulness (M = 4.05). These findings suggest
that low‐cost, embedded AI systems, designed with pedagogical

in engineering education.
The outcomes align closely with the instructional design's
constructivist
and
constructionist
principles.
Students
learned by building: creating tangible, rule‐driven systems
that reflected their decision‐making logic. The hands‐on
nature of the activity allowed abstract AI concepts, such as
inference engines, symbolic reasoning, and system dynamics,
to be internalized through iterative testing and debugging
cycles. There was an evident sense of competence and
autonomy by students, even as hardware limitations resulted
in design constraints.
These findings are consistent with previous studies that used
microcontroller‐based
expert
systems
for
education
(e.g.,
Udvaros et al. [7] and Mustofa et al. [8]), where students
demonstrated improved computational thinking and engage-
ment. However, BattleInTheSky embeds AI decision‐making
into a gamified, self‐contained console, offering symbolic rea-
soning practice and a multisensory learning experience that
reinforces system‐level thinking. Compared to other interven-
tions using the Pico W (e.g., Davidson et al. [14] and
Doropoulou et al. [15]), our approach emphasizes rule trans-
parency and ethical design, aligning with global calls for
transparency and interpretability in AI education.
From a technical perspective, the project demonstrated that
symbolic AI can be effectively implemented on constrained
microcontrollers, challenging the prevailing notion that mean-
ingful AI learning requires access to high‐end infrastructure.
The Raspberry Pi Pico W proved stable, programmable, and
responsive, supporting real‐time interactions and data storage
without reliance on cloud infrastructure. This resilience and
affordability position the platform as a viable entry point for AI
education in resource‐constrained contexts.
Regarding
scalability
and
sustainability,
BattleInTheSky
proved feasible across different educational settings. The sys-
tem relies entirely on open‐source hardware and software,
with an approximate cost of USD $15/unit. Its components are
reusable and locally available, and the platform can operate
offline using only the Thonny IDE and MicroPython. From a
technical
scalability
perspective,
the
modular
rule‐based
architecture allows for efficient expansion: for instance, the
inference engine handles increasing rule complexity without
significant performance degradation, as demonstrated by low
memory usage (~14 KB) and consistent latencies (12–27 ms),
even with chained inferences and multiple sensors (Table 1
and Figure 2). This enables scaling to more advanced imple-
mentations, such as integrating additional hardware (sensors
for multiplayer modes), or deploying in networked environ-
ments via WiFi, while maintaining responsiveness in resource‐
constrained microcontrollers. This modular, low‐cost design
supports replication in classrooms with limited resources, and
adaptation to remote or hybrid learning environments (such as
virtual simulations using MicroPython emulators for online
platforms) confirming the project's potential to democratize
AI education.
These results have broader implications for engineering and
computer science curriculum design. Educators can bridge
the gap between theory and practice by integrating embedded
expert systems as learning tools while promoting transpar-
ency and interpretability in AI systems. The rule‐based
nature of the projects also encourages ethical reflection, as
students must design clear, traceable decision logic. Such
experiences can complement advanced machine learning
courses by cultivating a foundational understanding of
AI logic and system design.
In the Latin American context, where digital inequities persist,
the project's use of low‐cost Raspberry Pi Pico W provides a
scalable model for AI education, addressing technological
access barriers [34]. Students found the hands‐on approach
more accessible than traditional lectures (“The game made me
think like an AI engineer”), aligning with AI‐driven pedagogi-
cal innovation [35]. The curriculum's focus on explainable AI,
emphasizing transparent IF–THEN rules to avoid bias, responds
to global calls for responsible AI use [36, 37]. Classroom dis-
cussions on algorithmic fairness further reinforced ethical
awareness.
Despite its strengths, the study is not without limitations. The
sample was relatively small and context‐specific, limited to
one institution and course. Evaluation focused on short‐term
outcomes, and longer‐term retention or knowledge transfer
was not assessed. Furthermore, although care was taken to
scaffold tasks equitably, students with more substantial prior
experience may have influenced team performance. Future
studies should explore longitudinal impacts, deploy the
approach across diverse institutions, and investigate how
team size and prior knowledge variations affect learning
outcomes.
BattleInTheSky illustrates how embedded expert systems can
democratize AI education by making symbolic reasoning visi-
ble, tangible, and accessible. The project provides a scalable,
adaptable model for inclusive and ethical AI learning in en-
gineering contexts by uniting open‐source tools, pedagogical
theory, and affordable hardware.

Conclusions
This study demonstrates the potential of embedded expert sys-
tems as powerful pedagogical tools for teaching AI in en-
gineering education. Unlike traditional approaches that often
rely on abstract theory or complex machine learning models,
BattleInTheSky offers a novel framework that bridges theory
and practice through a unique integration of symbolic reason-
ing, tangible interaction, and gamified design. The measurable
learning gains, strong motivation scores, and high‐quality arti-
facts validate the effectiveness of this hands‐on, rule‐based
approach.
The use of the Raspberry Pi Pico W was central to the project's
success, offering a reliable and low‐cost platform that supports
real‐time interaction and transparent AI logic. Its affordability
and simplicity allowed students to focus on the logic and design
of expert systems rather than technical complexity, making AI
education more equitable and practical, particularly in regions
where digital infrastructure remains limited.
Beyond its technical and educational contributions, the proj-
ect also fostered a deeper form of ethical reflection by
requiring students to design interpretable systems grounded
on IF–THEN rules (that is, explicit rule‐based decision
structures whose internal logic can be examined, explained,
and justified). Classroom discussions on algorithmic fairness
and bias complemented this technical component, reinforcing
the importance of transparent, interpretable AI systems
[particulary in educational context, where accountability and
clarity in decision processes are essential). This alignment
between pedagogical theory, social relevance, and hands‐on
practice underscores the broader educational significance of
the project.
Future work should focus on scaling the approach to different
educational levels and contexts, exploring longitudinal impacts,
and expanding the system's capabilities through sensors, col-
laboration, or integration with other AI paradigms. As calls for
responsible, inclusive AI education continue to grow, projects
like BattleInTheSky offer scalable, contextualized solutions that
bridge theory and practice while empowering the next genera-
tion of engineers.

Abstract: Expert systems are a core branch of Artificial Intelligence (AI), but they are often taught through abstract theory that hinders students' understanding and motivation. This study presents BattleInTheSky, a gamified expert system implemented on the low‐cost Raspberry Pi Pico W microcontroller using MicroPython. Designed as a hands‐on learning tool for Mechatronics Engineering students, the system uses IF–THEN rules to control hardware components including buttons, an OLED display, and a buzzer. It stores gameplay statistics locally and optionally uploads data remotely, providing an interactive experience that connects AI theory to practical applications. The project integrates symbolic AI, embedded programming, gamification, and principals of ethical design. It was implemented through a constructivist learning sequence in a sixth‐semester Expert System course, guiding students from basic hardware control to the design of fully functional expert systems. A mixed‐methods evaluation assessed technical performance and educational impact. Results showed that students improved their understanding of expert systems by 22.4% (Cohen's d = 1.3) and reported high motivation (mean 4.0/5). Technical evaluation confirmed the system's reliability, responsiveness, and usability in classroom settings. The project also fostered ethical reflection through rule transparency and responsible decision‐making logic. BattleInTheSky demonstrates how low‐cost, transparent, and rule‐based AI systems can promote accessible and engaging AI education. The approach illustrates how transparent, rule‐based systems can support explainable and accessible engineering and computing courses, particularly in resource‐constrained contexts.
